items.name: Extra shelf-stable food you already eat
items.why: Adds 0.9 days of food for 3 people, bringing you to 5.1 of the 7-day goal. About 10 of 100 households like yours can't get to a store for 3 days or more in the next 10 years. Main causes here: pandemic and supply chain disruption.

items.name: Phone power bank (about 20,000 mAh)
items.why: Adds half a day of phone power and news, which completes the 2-day goal. About 9 of 100 households like yours lose phone and internet for a day or more in the next 10 years. Main causes here: strong wind and hurricane. Also helps with power cuts.

items.name: Extra shelf-stable food you already eat
items.why: Adds 1.9 days of food for 3 people, which completes the 7-day goal. About 5 of 100 households like yours can't get to a store for 5 days or more in the next 10 years. Main causes here: pandemic and supply chain disruption.

savings_track.why: Of 100 households like yours, about 15 (7–30) will have an income gap of more than 3 months in the next 10 years. The goal is about 2.5 months of expenses (about $17,500); you have 4 months saved. You already have enough saved for this goal. This is a savings goal, kept separate from the supplies budget.

requirements.plain: 2 battery lights: a headlamp or lantern for each person aged 4 and over. Use lights, not candles. (Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)
1 pack of AA or AAA batteries for the lights and the radio: one pack lasts a household about 7 days. Check which sizes your lights use. (Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)

1 pair of appliance thermometers, one in the fridge and one in the freezer: after a power cut, keep refrigerated food only if it stayed at 40 °F or below, and throw out perishable food that was above 40 °F for 2 hours or more. (Ready.gov)

1 battery power station (about 1,070 Wh each) to keep refrigerated medicine cool through a 5-day power cut, because a cooler bag lasts only about 1 day. Your essential load (phones) is about 30 Wh a day, 150 Wh for 5 days; one station gives about 910 Wh after losses, enough for about 30.3 days of that load. A full-size fridge alone would drain one in about 0.9 days. It can run a small 12-volt cooler for the medicine, or the fridge in short spells. Recharge it from a car, gas or electric, with the engine running outdoors only, or from a solar panel. (retail prices, ENERGY STAR, CDC; some amounts are estimates)

Optional: a portable generator can run the fridge and lights through a 5-day outage. It must run outdoors, at least 20 feet from windows, doors and vents, never in a garage, and it needs fuel (see the fuel line). (CDC, Ready.gov, Ready Reckoner research; some amounts are estimates)

Optional: keeping a fridge running takes about 995 Wh a day (a chest freezer about 597) × 5 days = 4,980 Wh. A closed fridge keeps food cold about 4 hours and a full freezer about 48; shelf-stable food avoids the need. (ENERGY STAR, Ready.gov)

For a boil-water notice of up to 5 days: make about 5.1 gallons of drinking water safe each day, about 25.3 gallons in all. To make it safe, boil it for 1 minute (3 minutes above 5,000 feet), or add 8 drops of 6 % unscented bleach per gallon (6 drops of 8.25 %) and wait 30 minutes; double the bleach for cloudy or very cold water. A gas stove can boil water while the gas flows; never use a camp stove or grill indoors. (Ready.gov, CDC, NCA5 Atlas, AAP; some amounts are estimates)

1 bottle of plain unscented bleach (5 to 9 % sodium hypochlorite, not the splashless kind), for making water safe and for cleaning, however long your target is. At about 0.5 mL a gallon, each ounce treats about 60 gallons of clear water (30 if it is cloudy or very cold), so one bottle treats thousands of gallons. Bleach weakens in storage: buy a fresh bottle every 6 months, when you replace the water you store yourself. (CDC, EPA; some amounts are estimates)

If you boil on a camp stove outdoors, about 3.5 lb of propane brings 96 L to a boil (about 25 to 30 L a pound). Never use a camp stove indoors, and keep no more than 2 one-pound cylinders inside. (EIA, local fire code, CDC; some amounts are estimates)

3 people × 1.75 gallons a day × 2 days = 10.5 gallons, plus 0.5 gallons to mix formula, plus 0.6 gallons for the dog: about 11.6 gallons. Your county has at least 30 days a year at 95 °F or more, and drinking water can double in heat, so each person gets 1.75 gallons a day. Replace water you store yourself every 6 months. (Ready.gov, CDC, NCA5 Atlas, AAP; some amounts are estimates)

Free first step: fill clean drink bottles you already have with tap water, about 6 gallons, the most a household can usually gather this way. Not milk jugs: they leak. Label them and replace the water every 6 months. (Ready Reckoner research, CDC, Ready.gov, Church of Jesus Christ; some amounts are estimates)
A two-bucket toilet for when toilets can't flush: 2 sturdy buckets with a seat, one for pee and one for poo. (RDPO, Oregon OEM)

Toilet bags: about 0.45 heavy garbage bags a person a day (0.3 to 0.6), counting both bags of a double-bagged load: 2 people × 2 days = 2 bags. Fill halfway, tie, double-bag, and store away from food, water, children and pets. Don't put them in curbside trash or bury them unless officials say so. (RDPO, Oregon OEM; some amounts are estimates)

Cover material for the poo bucket (sawdust, shredded paper, dry leaves or pet bedding): about 1 cup a person a day (0.5 to 1.5) × 2 people × 2 days = 4 cups, about 0.3 gallons. (RDPO; some amounts are estimates)

2 adults at about 2,262 kcal a day each: about 4,523 kcal a day × 7 days = 31,700 kcal. These are moderately active needs; the form does not ask sex, so men's and women's needs are averaged. Count calories, not servings. Babies under 1 are fed breast milk or formula (see the formula line). (Dietary Guidelines)

As everyday groceries: about $130 for 14 person-days (USDA Thrifty Food Plan, $8.44 a person a day, plus 10 % for a household of 2). Buy what you already eat, keep it in the pantry and use the oldest first. (USDA)

As bulk staples such as wheat, rice and beans: about $35 ($2.15 to $2.85 a person a day). Cheapest, but it needs cooking and is short on some vitamins, so it suits months rather than days. (Church of Jesus Christ, BYU)

As freeze-dried or dehydrated meals: about $380 ($9 to $39 per 2,000 kcal, so $142 to $617). They need about 0.6 gallons of extra water a person a day to prepare. (Dietary Guidelines, retail prices; some amounts are estimates)

A retail "30-day" food kit supplies about 1,290 to 1,730 kcal a day. For the average person here (about 2,262 kcal a day) one lasts about 17 to 23 days, not 30. Compare kits by total kcal. (Dietary Guidelines, retail prices)

1 baby on formula: up to 32 oz of prepared formula a day, about 5 oz of powder (labels differ), × 7 days = 35 oz of powder. Ready-to-feed formula is safest in an emergency; powder needs safe water (counted in the water line). Check the amount every month as the baby grows. (AAP, CDC; some amounts are estimates)

Dry food for the dog for 7 days (at least a week): about 0.7 lb a day for each dog = 4.9 lb. Feed what the label says for yours, and keep it in an airtight, waterproof container. (ASPCA, Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)
Food for the dog for 7 days (7 pet-days, at least a week): what it eats now, in an airtight, waterproof container. (ASPCA, Ready.gov)

If you cook or boil water on a camp stove: about 0.2 lb of fuel a person a day × 3 people × 7 days = 4.2 lb, or 9 canisters of 0.5 lb each. Use it outdoors only, never indoors (carbon monoxide). (CDC, Ready Reckoner research, EIA, retail prices; some amounts are estimates)
Toilet paper: about 1 roll a person every 5 days × 2 people × 7 days = 3 rolls. Better still, measure a week's use and double it for two weeks. (Oregon OEM; some amounts are estimates)
Soap for 3 person-months: 3 people × 1 month. Each is 250 g of bathing soap and 200 g of laundry soap, about 1,350 g in all. (Sphere)

Period products for 2 cycles each, about 20 products a cycle (15 to 30). The form doesn't ask sex, so the plan counts half of the 2 people aged 13 to 64 who are not pregnant or nursing: 2 cycles' worth, about 40 products. Keep soap, clean underwear and pain relievers with them, and put used products in a separate bag. (CDC, Sphere, Oregon OEM; some amounts are estimates)
Diapers: about 8 a day for each baby (6 to 12; newborns use the most), × 7 days = 56 diapers. Keep at least one large pack on hand. (CDC, Sutter Health; some amounts are estimates)
Baby wipes: at least 2 packs for each child in diapers for up to 2 weeks: 2 packs. (CDC)

2 battery fans: 1 for the home plus 1 for the 1 person most at risk from heat (65 and over, babies, pregnancy). Fans help only while it is below 90 °F indoors; above that, go to a cooling centre. (CDC; some amounts are estimates)
3 cooling towels, one for each person: wet them and wear them on the neck in a heat wave. (an estimate)
A heat plan: find your nearest cooling centre (dial 2-1-1), pick the coolest room, cover sunny windows, and agree who checks on whom. Never leave people or pets in a closed car. (CDC, Ready.gov)
1 room thermometer in the room where the most vulnerable person sleeps: fans help only while it is below 90 °F indoors, so when it reads higher, go somewhere cooler. (CDC)
2 warm blankets, one for each person aged 1 and over: most homes already have them. Dress a baby in warm sleepwear or a sleep sack instead of loose blankets. (Ready.gov, Sphere, CDC)
3 sets of warm layers (coat, hat, gloves, dry socks), one for each person. (Ready.gov, CDC)
An upgrade, not a need: 2 sleeping bags or extra heavy blankets, one for each person. Blankets and warm layers cover a cold target of 3 days. (Ready.gov, Sphere; some amounts are estimates)

A cold plan: pick one room to keep warm, close off the others, put towels under doors and cover windows at night. Never heat with a gas oven, grill, camp stove or generator indoors (carbon monoxide). Gas, oil and propane furnaces usually need electricity for their fans and controls, so plan for cold without power. Babies under 1 should never sleep in a cold room. A body temperature below 95 °F needs medical help at once. (CDC; some amounts are estimates)

1 person takes prescription medicine every day: keep 10 days of it on hand. Keep a written list of each medicine, what it is for and the dose. After a disaster declaration some states let pharmacies give an emergency refill of up to 30 days, and many allow only a few days; ask your pharmacist what yours allows. (Florida DEM, CDC, Red Cross, Healthcare Ready)

1 person needs medicine kept cold, such as insulin. An insulated bag with fresh cold packs keeps it cool, never frozen, for about 1 day. Insulin in its vial or pen keeps working up to 28 days between 59 °F and 86 °F, so in a longer power cut keep it in the shade and below 86 °F; never use insulin that froze. Your power target is 5 days: plan a battery power station to run a small 12-volt cooler or the fridge (see its line), and a place with power you could go to. (FDA, CDC; some amounts are estimates)

No antibiotics are included in this plan. If you have a specific, foreseeable need, such as remote travel, talk to your own clinician about a standby prescription with written instructions. Never use fish or pet antibiotics, never share prescriptions, and don't use expired ones. (CDC, FDA)
1 battery or hand-crank radio that gets NOAA Weather Radio, with a tone alert, for warnings when phones and power are down. (Ready.gov, NOAA)
Power banks: 2 phones × about 15 Wh a day (10 to 20) × 5 days without power = 150 Wh. Text instead of calling to save battery. (Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)

2 two-way radios for the 2 people aged 13 and over, to reach each other when phones are down. FRS radios need no licence; GMRS radios reach farther but need a $35 FCC licence that covers the family for 10 years. (FCC; some amounts are estimates)
2 written contact cards, one for each person aged 4 and over: an out-of-area contact, meeting places and key numbers. Phones die; paper does not. (Ready.gov)
1 paper map of your area, marked with meeting places and ways out. Save offline maps on your phone too. (Ready.gov)

Cash in small bills, kept with your documents, because ATMs and cards may not work in an outage: about $100 to start, or enough for about 3 days of basics (food, fuel, medicine) at your own daily spending. No agency gives a dollar amount. (Ready.gov, FEMA; some amounts are estimates)

2 go-bags, one for each person aged 4 and over (babies' things go in a parent's bag): a sturdy bag you already own will do. Pack copies of documents, a phone charger, cash, a flashlight, a whistle, a change of clothes and sturdy shoes, and add water, food and medicines from your home supplies rather than buying them twice. You may get only minutes of warning (a local tsunami or a fast fire), so keep the bags packed by the door, and one at work if you work in a danger zone. Practise grabbing them and leaving. Plan where you would stay for about 3 days. (Washington EMD, Ready.gov, CDC; some amounts are estimates)

Water for the go-bags comes out of the water you store at home, not on top of it: the Red Cross three-day supply for leaving home, about 5.5 gallons a day for the 3 people × 3 days = 16.5 gallons. Keep it with the bags or take it as you leave. If you leave on foot, carry what you can (about 2.5 L each) and a filter; the rest goes in the car. (Red Cross, Washington EMD, Ready.gov, CDC; some amounts are estimates)

Food for the go-bags comes out of your home food supply, not on top of it: about 4,523 kcal a day × 3 days = 13,600 kcal of food that needs no cooking or refrigeration. (Red Cross, Washington EMD, Dietary Guidelines)

1 pet carrier, one for each pet, with a pet go-kit: water and food from your home supplies, any medicine it takes, records and a photo. Public shelters may take only service animals, so find pet-friendly places to stay ahead of time. (ASPCA, Ready.gov)
Water for the pet go-kit, set aside from your stored water rather than bought extra: 7 days for the dog = 2.2 gallons. Replace it every 2 months. (ASPCA, PetMD; some amounts are estimates)
Food for the pet go-kit, set aside from your pet food rather than bought extra: 10 days (7 to 10 days) for the dog = 10 pet-days. Replace it every 2 months. (ASPCA)

Keep both vehicles at least half full at all times, and fill up when leaving looks likely. Keep an electric car at least half charged too, and charge it fully when a storm is forecast. (Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)

Person 1 travels 19.9 miles (32 km) by car to work or school; walking home at about 3 mph takes about 6.6 hours. Keep a get-home bag in the car: comfortable walking shoes, a light, a paper map, cash in small bills, a rain or warm layer, and water and snacks from home. Be ready to stay at work for 24 hours if you can't leave. (FHWA, Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)

Water for person 1's walk home: 6.6 hours × about 0.71 L an hour in heat = 4.7 L, in a bottle filled from home rather than bought extra. Past about 2.5 L, carry a filter or purification tablets and an empty bottle instead of all the water. (FHWA, NIOSH; some amounts are estimates)

Snacks for person 1's walk home: about 700 kcal for 6.6 hours on foot (about 1,250 kcal every 12 hours), from your food at home rather than bought extra. (FHWA, Dietary Guidelines; some amounts are estimates)

Person 2 travels 5 miles (8 km) by car to work or school; walking home at about 3 mph takes about 1.7 hours. Keep a get-home bag in the car: comfortable walking shoes, a light, a paper map, cash in small bills, a rain or warm layer, and water and snacks from home. Be ready to stay at work for 24 hours if you can't leave. (FHWA, Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)
Water for person 2's walk home: 1.7 hours × about 0.71 L an hour in heat = 1.2 L, in a bottle filled from home rather than bought extra. (FHWA, NIOSH; some amounts are estimates)

Snacks for person 2's walk home: about 200 kcal for 1.7 hours on foot (about 1,250 kcal every 12 hours), from your food at home rather than bought extra. (FHWA, Dietary Guidelines; some amounts are estimates)
2 car emergency kits: jumper cables, a flashlight, warm clothes, a blanket, bottled water and snacks; sand or cat litter in snow country. (Ready.gov)

1 family first-aid kit for 3 people: the Red Cross list for a family of 4 (bandages, gauze, tape, antiseptic wipes, gloves, a breathing barrier, a cold pack, tweezers, an emergency blanket and a thermometer). Add your own medicines and emergency numbers, and replace what you use. (Red Cross)

1 package of each of 4 kinds of non-prescription medicine (a pain reliever, an anti-diarrhea medicine, an antacid and a laxative): one package of each lasts about 14 days for 4 people. That is 4 packages for 7 days. Follow the label, and ask a pharmacist about children's versions. (Ready.gov, Red Cross; some amounts are estimates)

N95 masks for wildfire smoke or an outbreak: 1 a day for each of the 2 people aged 4 and over, for 5 days = 10 masks. A well-fitting N95 protects more than a cloth or surgical mask. (CDC, Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)
1 oral thermometer (non-mercury, non-glass; it is on the Red Cross kit list) and 1 infant thermometer for the baby. (Red Cross, CDC)

Oral rehydration salts for vomiting, diarrhea or heat illness: 3 packets a person for every 2 weeks, at least 2 weeks' worth. For 3 people and 14 days that is 9 packets. Mix each packet into 1 litre of safe water. (CDC; some amounts are estimates)
1 bleeding-control kit: a tourniquet and a pressure bandage for serious bleeding, and a Stop the Bleed class so you know how to use them. Serious bleeding can kill before help arrives. (DHS)

A fire escape plan: two ways out of every room, a meeting spot outside, and a practice run with everyone. If anyone sleeps upstairs, check that each bedroom has a second way out, such as a window onto a porch roof or an escape ladder. Test your smoke alarms every month. (Ready.gov)

No fire extinguisher yet: 2 multipurpose (A-B-C) extinguishers, one on each of the 2 floors a home like yours has, the ground-floor one near the kitchen. If your kitchen is on another floor, keep one there too. Learn how to use one before you need it. Small home fires are common: CPSC estimated about 6.6 a year for every 100 households, most of them cooking fires, and fire departments attend only about 3 in 100 of them. (USFA, CPSC; some amounts are estimates)
Swap phone numbers with 2 neighbours and agree who checks on whom after a storm or an outage, when phones and roads may be down. (an estimate)

Savings goal: about 2.5 months of expenses ($17,500 at $7,000 a month), built up over time and kept apart from the supplies budget. You have about 4 months saved now. Planners often suggest 3 to 6 months; the CFPB says it depends on your situation. (FINRA, St. Louis Fed, CFPB)

Copy the 4 parts of FEMA's Emergency Financial First Aid Kit: IDs, financial and legal papers (including insurance), medical information, and household contacts. Keep copies in a waterproof, fire-resistant place or with someone you trust, with photos of your home and belongings, and update them once a year. (FEMA)

Home and renters policies usually don't cover floods. Decide on flood insurance before you need it: a new policy usually starts 30 days after you buy it. It pays up to $250,000 for the building and $100,000 for belongings. (FEMA, FloodSmart, Ready.gov)

packet_markdown:
# Your preparedness packet

**For:** 2 adults and 1 baby, with 1 dog  
**Where:** Fort Bend County, Texas (ZIP code 77479)  
**Home:** an owned house, with city water, gas heat and central air conditioning  
**Plan date:** October 1, 2026  
**Ready for:** serious disruptions, the kind that come about once in 50 years (the 1-in-50 setting), in the climate expected around 2050. Water is planned at the basic level, about 1 gallon a person a day.[1]

> Ready Reckoner is an independent, open-source planning aid. It is not official emergency guidance, and not medical, legal or financial advice. Follow instructions from your local officials first.

## Summary

**Where you are now:** getting started. **What is enough for your risks:** two weeks of supplies. At your budget, the plan gets there by month 5 (March 2027).

### The three things that matter most

1. Of 100 households like yours, about 25 (20–40) will have to leave home quickly at least once in the next 10 years. Know your evacuation zone and where you would go; leave when told.[2, 3]
2. Of 100 households like yours, about 70 (55–85) will lose grid power for a day or more in the next 10 years. If you are not told to leave, be ready to manage about 5 days at home with no power, and about 2 days with no tap water.
3. Of 100 households like yours, about 55 (30–90) will be unable to shop for food and supplies for 3 days or more in the next 10 years. Keep about 7 days of food you normally eat, and 10 days of daily medicine on hand.

### Start here

These cost nothing and come first. This month's 8 free steps are all under Your plan.

- [ ] Set up emergency alerts and know how to reach 911
- [ ] Make a household plan and a contact card for each person
- [ ] Fire safety at home: alarms, an escape plan, safe cooking and heating

### What the plan assumes you already have

- [x] A charged mobile phone: alerts, calls and a backup light (2 phones)
- [x] Go-bag for each person: a backpack you pack from your supplies (2 bags)
- [x] Manual can opener (1 opener)
- [x] A cooking pot with a lid (1 pot)
- [x] Three days of the food you normally eat (3 × 3 days of food for one person)
- [x] A warm blanket for each person (2 blankets)
- [x] Warm layers for each person: a coat, hat and gloves (3 sets)
- [x] Towels to wet and cool down (3 towels)

If any is missing, untick "Assume everyday basics" on the Have screen and the plan will add it.

## Your risks

What could reach a household like yours in Fort Bend County, Texas over the next 10 years: the likeliest events, and the rarer ones that can kill, most likely first. A lost job or a week-long outage is far more likely than a disaster from the movies, and the plan is ordered the same way.

### What to know and do

#### 1. Heat wave

Nearly every household like yours will go through a heat wave in a ten-year stretch around 2050 (about 1.5 times a year).[4, 5]

**What helps.** Know where you can go to cool off. Dial 2-1-1 to find air conditioning near you.[6] Cover windows with drapes or shades, and weather-strip doors and windows.[7] Take cool showers, wear loose, light-colored clothing, and drink plenty of fluids. Check on family members, older adults and neighbours.[7] Heat can cause power outages, so plan for refrigerated medicines and powered medical devices.[6] In a drought, follow local limits on water use, and make saving water a daily habit.[8]

**What to avoid.** Do not rely on a fan when it is over 90°F indoors. It can make you hotter.[6] Never leave people or pets in a closed car on a warm day.[7] Heat stroke is an emergency. Signs include a body temperature of 103°F or more, hot, red skin that may be dry or damp, a fast, strong pulse, confusion or passing out. Call 911, move the person somewhere cooler, cool them with cool cloths or a cool bath, and give them nothing to drink.[9]

**How bad:** Serious. **How sure:** Based on data.

#### 2. Medical emergency

Nearly every household like yours will have someone need emergency care in the next ten years (about 1.4 times a year).[10]

**What helps.** Take a first-aid and bleeding-control class. You may be able to save a life by acting right after an injury, before help arrives.[11] If a teen or adult collapses and their heart stops, call 911 and push hard and fast in the center of the chest. This hands-only CPR needs no training. Note where the nearest heart defibrillator (AED) is; it talks you through each step.[12] Keep a stocked first-aid kit. Check it regularly and replace anything used or out of date.[13] Keep a list of each person's medicines, doses and allergies with your emergency supplies.[14] Know how to reach 911. Call if you can, and text where that service works.[15]

**What to avoid.** Do not start antibiotics on your own or take someone else's. The wrong medicine can delay the right treatment and cause serious side effects.[16] Do not use expired medicines.[17]

**How bad:** Serious. **How sure:** Based on data.

#### 3. Job loss

Of 100 households like yours, about 81 will have someone lose a job in the next ten years.[18, 19]

**What helps.** Build an emergency fund a little at a time. The right amount depends on your situation.[20] Planners often suggest three to six months of living expenses, and more if your income varies.[21] Know how to file for unemployment in your state.[22] Keep copies of your financial, legal and medical papers together, with the names of people to call.[23] Write a bare-bones budget you could switch to, and keep a pantry that can stretch a tight month.

**What to avoid.** File soon after losing work: contact your state's unemployment program as soon as you can.[22] Do not keep your emergency fund in investments you would have to sell. A savings account lets you take money out at any time without a penalty.[21]

**How bad:** Serious. **How sure:** Mostly data.

#### 4. Hurricane

Of 100 households like yours, about 60 (38–81) will lose power or have damage from a hurricane or tropical storm in a ten-year stretch around 2050.[24, 25, 26, 27]

**What helps.** Know your evacuation zone, your routes and where you would stay. If you live in a mandatory evacuation zone and officials tell you to leave, go right away.[3] If you are not told to leave, shelter from the wind in a small inside room, closet or hallway away from windows, on the lowest floor that will not flood.[3, 28] Clear drains and gutters, bring in outdoor furniture, and think about storm shutters. Keep phones charged and have backup chargers.[3] A flood policy typically takes up to 30 days to start, so buy it well before a storm.[29] If you would leave in an electric car, keep it fully charged all hurricane season.[30]

**What to avoid.** Never walk or drive through floodwater. One foot of moving water can sweep a car away.[29] Do not drive or charge an electric car that has been in floodwater. Salt water can start a battery fire.[30] Never run a generator inside your home or garage.[31]

**How bad:** Serious. **How sure:** Mostly data.

#### 5. Death or disability of an earner

Of 100 households like yours, about 16 (10–26) will lose an earner's income to death or disability in the next ten years.[27, 32, 33]

**What helps.** The steps under "Job loss" above apply here too.

**How bad:** Very severe. **How sure:** Mostly data.

#### 6. Wildfire

Of 100 households like yours, about 4 (1–10) will have to leave home or lose power because of a wildfire in a ten-year stretch around 2050.[5, 24, 27]

**What helps.** Keep a zone at least 30 feet around your home clear of leaves, debris and anything that burns.[34] Know your evacuation zone and routes, and practice with your pets.[34] Store N95 masks for smoke. Pick a room you can close off from outside air, and run a portable air cleaner there.[34] N95 masks are not made to fit children, so for them the clean room is the protection.[35] A box fan with a MERV 13 filter makes a low-cost air cleaner.[36] If your heating and cooling system brings in fresh air, set it to recirculate.[34] Keep phones charged and have backup chargers.[34]

**What to avoid.** Leave as soon as authorities tell you to, even if you cannot see flames.[34] Do not use an air cleaner that makes ozone.[37] Avoid hard exercise when it is smoky, so you breathe in less smoke.[37]

**How bad:** Moderate. **How sure:** Rough data.

#### 7. Flooding from rivers or heavy rain

Of 100 households like yours, about 4 (1–9) will have flood water reach their home in a ten-year stretch around 2050.[5, 27, 38]

**What helps.** Look up your address on FEMA's flood maps, and sign up for your community's warnings.[29] Homeowner's insurance does not cover flooding, and a flood policy typically takes up to 30 days to start.[29] Renters can buy flood coverage for their belongings.[39] Know how you would get to higher ground or a higher floor.[29]

**What to avoid.** Six inches of moving water can knock you down, and one foot can sweep your car away.[29] Never drive around barriers on a flooded road. The road may have collapsed under the water.[40] Stay off bridges over fast-moving water.[29] Leave if you are told to.[41]

**How bad:** Very severe. **How sure:** Rough data.

#### 8. House fire

Of 100 households like yours, about 3 will have a house fire in the next ten years.[42]

**What helps.** Put smoke alarms inside and outside every bedroom and on every level, and test them each month.[43] Practice your escape plan twice a year, including finding your way out in the dark.[44] Sleep with bedroom doors closed. Teach children not to hide from firefighters.[44] If there is smoke, crawl low under it to your exit.[44] If you cannot get out, close the door, cover vents and cracks with cloth or tape, call 911, and signal from the window with a light-colored cloth or a flashlight.[44] Insurance and copies of your documents help you recover afterward.[23]

**What to avoid.** Before you open a door, feel the door and the knob. If either is hot, or smoke is coming around it, keep it closed and use your second way out.[44] If a person or pet is still inside, get out and tell firefighters right away.[44] If your clothes catch fire, stop, drop and roll.[44]

**How bad:** Severe. **How sure:** Based on data.

#### 9. Tornado

Of 100 households like yours, about 1 (fewer than 1 to 4) will have a tornado damage or cut off their neighborhood in the next ten years.[24, 27]

**What helps.** Pick your shelter spot now. A safe room or storm shelter is best.[45] The next best is a small, windowless room or basement on the lowest floor of a sturdy building.[45, 46] Sign up for your community's warnings, and learn what your sirens sound like.[45] Know the signs of a tornado: a rotating funnel cloud, a cloud of debris, or a roar like a freight train. ### No grid power at home: about 5 days (3–7)

**What helps.** Have a flashlight for each person.[59] Keep a battery or hand-crank radio, and a backup battery for each phone.[60] Keep the fridge and freezer closed. A closed fridge keeps food cold for about four hours, and a full freezer for about two days.[59] If someone relies on a powered medical device or cold medicine, make a plan with their medical provider now.[59] Join your power company's medical program for early warnings of outages, but plan as if your power will not come back first.[61] Many cities and counties keep a voluntary registry of people who may need help; ask yours.[14] A battery power station burns no fuel, so it makes no carbon monoxide.[31]

**What to avoid.** Never run a generator inside your home or garage, even with the doors and windows open. Keep it outside, more than 20 feet from windows, doors and vents.[31] Put a carbon monoxide alarm on every level of your home.[59] Headache, dizziness, nausea or confusion can mean carbon monoxide poisoning. Get everyone outside to fresh air, then call 911.[62] Never heat your home with a gas stove or oven. Unplug electronics, because the power can come back with a surge that damages them.[59] Treat every downed power line as live: stay at least 30 feet from it and anything it touches, and call 911.[63] If one falls on your car, stay inside unless the car is on fire.[64]

### Tap water must be treated: about 5 days (3–10)

**What helps.** Use bottled water, or bring clear water to a rolling boil for one minute. Boil for three minutes above 5,000 feet, then let it cool.[65] If you cannot boil water, add plain unscented bleach: 8 drops of 6% bleach or 6 drops of 8.25% bleach per gallon. Stir, and wait 30 minutes.[65] Use boiled or bottled water for drinking, cooking, brushing teeth, baby formula and ice. If the power is out too, a camp stove works, but only outdoors.[31]

**What to avoid.** Do not use water or ice from the fridge dispenser while a notice is on. Boil tap water even if it went through a home filter or a filter pitcher.[66] Boiling does not help if the notice warns of chemicals. That is a do-not-drink notice, and you need stored or bottled water instead.[66, 67]

### No tap water at all: about 2 days (1–5)

**What helps.** Store at least one gallon per person per day, for drinking and keeping clean.[1] Fill clean bottles or jugs with tap water and replace it every six months.[68] You can pick a level in the plan. About 3 liters a day covers drinking to survive, one gallon is the basic default, and about 4 gallons (15 liters) is the humanitarian minimum for drinking, cooking and washing.[69] A tank water heater holds 20 to 80 gallons of clean water.[70, 71] For long outages, a filter and a source of raw water go further than more jugs.[58] Filters do not remove viruses, so add a disinfectant such as chlorine dioxide after filtering.[67] A two-bucket toilet keeps waste safe when toilets cannot flush.[72]

**What to avoid.** Do not store water in containers that held chemicals.[68] Milk jugs seal poorly and turn brittle.[73] Never drink pool or spa water. Use it only for washing and cleaning.[71] After a flood, do not drink from a private well until it has been disinfected and tested. Your health department can tell you how.[74]

### Can't get to a store: about 7 days (5 days to 3 weeks)

**What helps.** Keep extra food that needs no refrigeration, cooking or water, and choose foods your family will eat.[75] Use the oldest cans first and replace them as you go.[76] Buy a little at a time. Ready.gov asks people to buy supplies slowly, so everyone can get what they need.[77] Keep a manual can opener.[75] The plan counts food in calories, not servings. Many "30-day" meal kits hold only about 1,300 to 1,700 calories a day.[78] That is less than most adults need.[79] Store food somewhere cool and dry. Below 85°F is best.[76]

**What to avoid.** Do not buy everything at once. It strains your budget and the store. Do not buy or eat from cans that bulge, leak, are rusted or are deeply dented.[76] Do not trust a kit's "days" label. Check the calories on the package instead.

### Dangerous heat or cold indoors: about 3 days (2–5)

**What helps.** Agree who checks on whom, especially older neighbours and anyone who lives alone.[6, 80] In heat, go where there is air conditioning. Dial 2-1-1 to find one.[6] Cover windows with drapes or shades.[7] In cold, close off rooms you don't need, stuff towels under doors, and cover windows with blankets at night. Have extra blankets, sleeping bags and warm coats.[80] Babies under one year old should never sleep in a cold room.[80] If you cannot keep your home warm, go to a warming center. Dial 2-1-1 to find one.[81] If you heat with wood, have the stove and chimney professionally inspected and cleaned every year, because creosote from the smoke builds up and can start a fire.[82]

**What to avoid.** Fans move air but do not lower body temperature.[7] Above 90°F indoors, a fan can make you hotter.[6] Never heat your home with a gas oven, and never use a grill or camp stove indoors.[31] Headache, dizziness, nausea or confusion can mean carbon monoxide poisoning: get outside, then call 911.[62] Keep space heaters 3 feet from anything that can burn.[83] Never leave people or pets in a closed car on a warm day.[7]

### Medication and medical-supply continuity: about 10 days (7 days to 3 weeks)

**What helps.** Refill early, while you still have a week left. The Red Cross suggests keeping a 7-day supply, and Florida advises at least two weeks.[84, 85] Ask your doctor, pharmacist and drug plan how to build an emergency supply, such as a 90-day fill.[14, 86] Keep a written list of each person's medicines, doses and allergies.[14] Many states let pharmacists give an emergency refill, but the rules differ.[87] After a declared disaster, a federal program can help people without insurance replace prescriptions.[88] People with diabetes should pack supplies for at least 1 to 2 weeks: syringes or pen needles, a glucose meter with test strips and spare batteries, and glucose tablets.[89, 90] Insulin in its original vial or pen, opened or not, keeps working for up to 28 days at 59°F to 86°F. In an outage, keep it below 86°F in the shade or a cooler, never frozen.[91, 92] For other medicines that need a fridge, ask your pharmacist now how long each keeps out of it, and write the answer on your medicine list.[59]

**What to avoid.** Do not throw insulin away after a day without power. If it gets hotter than 86°F and you have nothing else, use it, and replace it as soon as you can.[91] Never use insulin that has frozen or looks unusual, with particles, clumps, crystals or a changed color.[91, 93] Do not use expired medicines. Weak antibiotics can fail to treat an infection.[17] Do not share antibiotics or save them for later.[16]

### No phone, internet or card payments: about 2 days (1–5)

**What helps.** Turn on emergency alerts on every phone. They are free, and you do not need to sign up.[94] Keep a battery or hand-crank radio and a NOAA Weather Radio with a tone alert.[60] NOAA Weather Radio has more than 1,000 transmitters covering all 50 states.[95] Write important phone numbers on paper, not only in your phone.[96] Pick an out-of-state contact everyone can text, and a place to meet if you are separated.[97] Keep some cash in small bills, because ATMs and credit cards may not work.[98] License-free two-way radios (FRS) let family members talk over short distances without a phone network.[99]

**What to avoid.** Do not rely on one source of news. Do not assume you can text 911 everywhere. It is not available in every area, so call 911 if you can.[15]

### Must leave home quickly

**What helps.** See the steps under Family plan.

**What to avoid.** Many people wait to check with others before they act on a warning.[100] Always follow the instructions of local officials, and leave early enough to avoid being trapped by bad weather.[2] Never walk or drive through floodwater. Six inches of moving water can knock you down.[29]

### Stranded away from home

**What helps.** See the steps under Family plan.

**What to avoid.** Do not force down water when you are not thirsty. Too much water can be harmful.[101] In heat, do not drink more than 6 cups an hour.[102] If you are stuck in a car in a snowstorm, staying in the car is often safest. Run the engine about 10 minutes an hour with a window cracked, and keep the exhaust pipe clear of snow.[80]

### Medical emergency when help is slow

**What helps.** See "Medical emergency" under Your risks.

### House fire

**What helps.** Put smoke alarms inside and outside sleeping areas and on every level of your home. Test them every month.[43] Some fire departments and the Red Cross install them for free.[43, 103] If you rent, ask your landlord to put them in.[104] Make an escape plan with two ways out of each room, and practice it twice a year.[44] Cooking left alone is the top cause of kitchen fires that spread beyond the pan, so stay with your cooking. Keep a pan lid or baking sheet nearby to cover a pan that catches fire.[105] Keep anything that can burn at least 3 feet from heaters, fireplaces and candles.[83] A multipurpose extinguisher labeled "A-B-C" works on most home fires.[106]

**What to avoid.** If a person or pet is still inside, get out, call 911, and tell firefighters where they are.[44] Never heat your home with an oven.[83] Turn off space heaters when you leave the room or go to bed.[83] Replace 9-volt alarm batteries at least once a year.[43] If you smell gas or hear hissing, get everyone out without touching switches or phones, then call 911 and the gas company from a safe distance.[107, 108] Only a professional should turn the gas back on.[108]

### Home and personal security

**What helps.** Burglars look for homes that are easy targets. Lock up, and light the places where someone could hide.[109] Work with your neighbours to look out for each other.[109] Protect key accounts with a password manager and two-step login.[110] Learn a simple way to handle a tense moment: notice what is happening, say hello, judge the risk, and get help if you need it.[111] If an attack happens in a public place, getting away is the top priority.[112]

**What to avoid.** After a disaster, be careful with people who show up offering fast repairs or help for a fee. Report scams at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.[113] Do not hide a spare key under the doormat or a planter. Leave it with a trusted neighbour.[109]

### Contacts and meeting places

- **Make a household plan and a contact card for each person.** Agree how you will reach each other, where you will meet if you are separated, and who picks up the children (Ready.gov). Pick one out-of-state contact everyone texts to say they are safe, since texts often get through when calls do not, and write key numbers on a card for each wallet or bag (Ready.gov). Add school, daycare and work plans, and go over the plan together once a year.[23, 96, 97, 123, 127, 128]

- **Set up emergency alerts and know how to reach 911.**

### Leaving home: triggers and routes

About 25 of 100 households like yours have to leave home quickly at least once in 10 years. Warning can be 1 minute to 3 days ahead. Plan to be away for about 3 days.[5, 24, 25, 26, 27, 38, 42, 51, 52]

- **Plan how you would leave: zone, routes, destination and triggers.** Look up your evacuation zone and routes on your state and county emergency management websites, mark two routes on a paper map, and pick where you would go, pet-friendly if you have pets (Ready.gov). For each likely hazard, write a go-or-stay card and an if-then trigger, such as 'If our zone gets an evacuation warning, we leave within 30 minutes.' Plans written in if-then form make people more likely to follow through.[2, 3, 60, 100, 129, 130, 131, 132]
- **Keep your vehicle ready: half a tank, a charged battery, a good spare.** Keep at least half a tank of gas at all times and a full tank when an evacuation looks likely (Ready.gov); if you drive an electric car, keep it charged through storm season and pick destinations within its range (Hillsborough County, Florida). Check the spare tire with the others each month, and keep a phone charging cable in the car (NHTSA). Run the engine only outdoors, never in a garage (CDC).[2, 30, 31, 121, 133, 134, 135, 136]

- **Practice: ten-minute drills and the first things to do.**

#### Drills and if-then plans

**If-then plans.** An if-then plan links a trigger to an action: "If the county issues an evacuation warning for our zone, we leave within 30 minutes." Plans written this way help people follow through.[131] When a warning comes, people often wait to confirm it with others before they act.[100] A trigger you agreed on earlier leaves less to decide in the moment. Write one for each likely hazard, and add who picks up the children and where you will meet.[127]

**Drills.** In New Zealand, people who took part in earthquake drills knew the right actions better, used them more during real shaking, and did more to prepare.[137] Among people who got out of the World Trade Center on 9/11, those with earlier emergency training were less likely to develop PTSD.[138] Practice your fire escape plan twice a year.[44] Other ten-minute drills: Drop, Cover and Hold On, a night without power, grabbing the go-bag against a timer, and sealing a room to shelter in place.[132]

**What to avoid.** Do not skip drills because they feel silly. Each one you finish counts toward your plan.

### Children

#### Talking with children about emergencies

**Before anything happens.** Let children help build the kit and practice the plan.[139] Make sure each child knows your family meeting place and has a contact card.[127] Practice the fire escape plan together twice a year.[44]

**When something happens.** Start by asking what they already know and what questions they have. Give simple, concrete facts without scary details. For a young child, that might be: "A tree branch fell on the power lines, so the lights are off." Tell them about the many people working to help, and the steps being taken to keep them safe.[140]

**What to avoid.** Limit news coverage. If children watch, watch with them and answer their questions.[140] Reassure them when you honestly can, but do not give false reassurance. Let them know it is all right to be upset. If you feel overwhelmed, get support from another adult first. Helping others in the community can ease a child's sense of helplessness.[140]

### Neighbors

- **Neighbours and skills: swap numbers, check on each other, learn first aid.**

#### Neighbours and mutual aid

**What helps.** Swap phone numbers with two neighbours. Agree who checks on whom, especially older neighbours and anyone who lives alone. Make a simple contact list for your street. Give a trusted person a spare key, and tell them where your supplies are and how to use any medical equipment.[141] Host a block party, since strong communities start with prepared neighbours.[142] Take CERT training to learn fire safety, light search and rescue, and disaster first aid.[143]

**What to avoid.** Meet the people next door before you need them. A short hello now makes it easier to knock on a door later.

### Pets

- **Pet plan: microchip, records, a photo and a buddy.** Keep your pet's ID tag and microchip details current, put vaccination records and a recent photo with your documents, and arrange a buddy who can care for or evacuate your pets if you cannot (Ready.gov). If officials ask you to evacuate, your pets should go too.[129, 130]

## Documents and money

Keep paper copies in a waterproof pouch and photos you can reach from any phone. FEMA's Emergency Financial First Aid Kit groups them in four parts.[23]

- [ ] **Who you are:** photo IDs, birth certificates, Social Security cards, passports, and pet records.
- [ ] **Money and legal papers:** insurance policies, the lease or deed, bank and card contact numbers (not PINs), and recent tax returns.
- [ ] **Medical papers:** insurance cards, the written medicine list, prescriptions, and vaccination records.
- [ ] **Contacts:** family, doctors, the insurance agent, the landlord or lender, and employers.

- **Documents and insurance: copy key papers, record belongings, check cover.** Use FEMA's Emergency Financial First Aid Kit to gather IDs, financial and legal papers, insurance, medical information and contacts, and photograph or video every room and valuable item. Keep paper copies in a waterproof bag and another copy with someone you trust or in secure online storage (FEMA). Check what your insurance covers: standard home and renters policies do not cover flood or earthquake damage, a new flood policy usually takes 30 days to start, and renters can buy their own policy and contents-only flood cover (Ready.gov, FEMA).[23, 29, 39, 60, 97, 98, 144, 145]
- **Fire-resistant, waterproof document pouch.** A fire-resistant, water-resistant pouch or small case for paper copies of key documents, a USB drive and some cash, easy to grab when you leave (FEMA's financial kit suggests fire- and waterproof storage).[23, 126]

### Insurance questions

- Home and renters policies usually don't cover floods. Decide on flood insurance before you need it: a new policy usually starts 30 days after you buy it. It pays up to $250,000 for the building and $100,000 for belongings. (FEMA, FloodSmart, Ready.gov)[39, 98, 144]

### Cash

- Cash in small bills, kept with your documents, because ATMs and cards may not work in an outage: about $100 to start, or enough for about 3 days of basics (food, fuel, medicine) at your own daily spending. No agency gives a dollar amount. (Ready.gov, FEMA; some amounts are estimates)[4, 23, 24, 25, 26, 27, 49, 50, 98, 121]

### Savings

Of 100 households like yours, about 15 (7–30) will have an income gap of more than 3 months in the next 10 years. The goal is about 2.5 months of expenses (about $17,500); you have 4 months saved. You already have enough saved for this goal. This is a savings goal, kept separate from the supplies budget.

- **Money: start an emergency fund and a bare-bones budget.** Set up an automatic transfer, however small, into a savings account you keep for emergencies; the CFPB says the right amount depends on your situation, and planners often suggest working toward three to six months of expenses (FINRA). Write down your essential monthly costs and what you would cut first, so you know how far savings would stretch. If anyone earns, find your state's unemployment website now, so you could file right away if a job ends (Department of Labor).[18, 20, 21, 22, 146, 147]

## Special needs

### Medicine

- 1 person takes prescription medicine every day: keep 10 days of it on hand. Keep a written list of each medicine, what it is for and the dose. After a disaster declaration some states let pharmacies give an emergency refill of up to 30 days, and many allow only a few days; ask your pharmacist what yours allows. (Florida DEM, CDC, Red Cross, Healthcare Ready)[4, 24, 25, 26, 27, 42, 49, 50, 51, 53, 54, 84, 85, 87, 89, 115, 148]
- 1 person needs medicine kept cold, such as insulin. An insulated bag with fresh cold packs keeps it cool, never frozen, for about 1 day. Insulin in its vial or pen keeps working up to 28 days between 59 °F and 86 °F, so in a longer power cut keep it in the shade and below 86 °F; never use insulin that froze. Your power target is 5 days: plan a battery power station to run a small 12-volt cooler or the fridge (see its line), and a place with power you could go to. (FDA, CDC; some amounts are estimates)[4, 5, 24, 25, 26, 27, 49, 50, 91, 92, 115, 121, 149, 150]

- **Keep medicines going: a written list, early refills, an emergency supply.** Write a paper list of each person's medicines with the dose their prescriber set, allergies, and the prescriber's and pharmacy's numbers, and keep copies in the go-bag and with your documents (Ready.gov). If anyone takes a daily medicine, refill when a week is left and ask the prescriber and pharmacist how to build an emergency supply; some states allow emergency refills, and a federal program can help people without insurance after a disaster. Set up telehealth and pharmacy logins now, and put spare glasses in the go-bag (Ready.gov).[14, 17, 23, 60, 84, 87, 88, 148, 151]
- **Insulated bag and cold packs for refrigerated medicine.** An insulated bag with cold packs keeps medicine such as insulin in the shade and below 86°F, never frozen, for about a day when the power is out or you leave home. Insulin in its vial or pen keeps working for up to 28 days between 59°F and 86°F (FDA, CDC); for any other medicine that must stay cold, ask your pharmacist how long it keeps out of the fridge. Pack diabetes supplies with it for 1 to 2 weeks: a glucose meter with test strips and lancets, syringes or pen needles, glucose tablets or another quick sugar, ketone strips and spare batteries (CDC).[89, 91, 92, 121, 126]

### Antibiotics

- No antibiotics are included in this plan. If you have a specific, foreseeable need, such as remote travel, talk to your own clinician about a standby prescription with written instructions. Never use fish or pet antibiotics, never share prescriptions, and don't use expired ones. (CDC, FDA)[16, 17, 152, 153]

### Babies and toddlers

- 1 baby on formula: up to 32 oz of prepared formula a day, about 5 oz of powder (labels differ), × 7 days = 35 oz of powder. Ready-to-feed formula is safest in an emergency; powder needs safe water (counted in the water line). Check the amount every month as the baby grows. (AAP, CDC; some amounts are estimates)[4, 24, 25, 26, 27, 53, 54, 121, 154, 155, 156, 157]
- Diapers: about 8 a day for each baby (6 to 12; newborns use the most), × 7 days = 56 diapers. Keep at least one large pack on hand. (CDC, Sutter Health; some amounts are estimates)[4, 24, 25, 26, 27, 53, 54, 121, 155, 157, 158]
- Baby wipes: at least 2 packs for each child in diapers for up to 2 weeks: 2 packs. (CDC)[4, 24, 25, 26, 27, 53, 54, 155, 157]
- 1 oral thermometer (non-mercury, non-glass; it is on the Red Cross kit list) and 1 infant thermometer for the baby. (Red Cross, CDC)[13, 155]

- **Pack an infant go-kit from CDC's checklist.** Use CDC's emergency checklist for families with infants: formula or breastfeeding supplies, diapers and wipes, an infant thermometer, a bulb syringe, a pain reliever made for infants, warm sleepwear or a sleep sack, and a portable crib. Babies under one should never sleep in a cold room (CDC).[80, 155]

### Pets and animals

- Dry food for the dog for 7 days (at least a week): about 0.7 lb a day for each dog = 4.9 lb. Feed what the label says for yours, and keep it in an airtight, waterproof container. (ASPCA, Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)[4, 24, 25, 26, 27, 53, 54, 121, 129, 130, 157]
- 1 pet carrier, one for each pet, with a pet go-kit: water and food from your home supplies, any medicine it takes, records and a photo. Public shelters may take only service animals, so find pet-friendly places to stay ahead of time. (ASPCA, Ready.gov)[2, 130]
- Water for the pet go-kit, set aside from your stored water rather than bought extra: 7 days for the dog = 2.2 gallons. Replace it every 2 months. (ASPCA, PetMD; some amounts are estimates)[121, 130, 159]
- Food for the pet go-kit, set aside from your pet food rather than bought extra: 10 days (7 to 10 days) for the dog = 10 pet-days. Replace it every 2 months. (ASPCA)[130]

### Stress and mental health

#### Stress, mental health and the 988 line

**What helps.** Save 988 in every phone. It offers free, judgment-free support 24/7 for mental health, substance use and more, by call, text or chat.[160] After a disaster, the Disaster Distress Helpline offers crisis counseling 24/7 to anyone in emotional distress. Call or text 1-800-985-5990.[161] Write a short calm plan: what you might feel, what helps you, and who you will call.[132] Oregon's 2 Weeks Ready program even includes practicing mindfulness as a step in getting prepared.[162]

**What to avoid.** Do not keep the news on all day. No one, adult or child, benefits from graphic details or disturbing images.[140] Reach out before things feel unbearable. The 988 line supports people in emotional distress as well as in crisis.[160]
